meta.title: How sponsors created value in home-services and adjacent companies: merged case set, common levers, chronological patterns and a dated Punctual Pros sequence
meta.author: Syed Rahman
meta.method: Merged the 17 home-services cases (cases_home_services.json) and 17 cross-sector cases (cases_cross_sector.json) into one set. De-duplication was by normalised company name; no company appeared in both files, so all 34 cases are kept with every original field preserved. Each case gains confidence (high = SEC/Companies House filings or sponsor releases with disclosed figures; medium = sponsor/company releases and trade press with figures undisclosed or press-estimated; low = few primary sources or reliance on search summaries), confidence basis, related cases, PE landscape links (sponsor ids in pe_landscape.json) and, where one exists, a portal view. Levers and patterns were derived from the dated timelines, levers used and KPI before/after of the 34 cases; every evidence row carries the source URL of the case timeline or KPI it came from. Timing statistics were computed in Python from timeline dates (months = days / 30.44; year-only dates use 1 July). Cross-references to Punctual Pros nationwide plan (pn-*), ServiceOS evidence (ve-*, kb-*) and Punctual Pros filings (pp-fil-*) reuse those items' source URL and retrieved dates. No new web retrieval was done for this merge; underlying pages were retrieved 2026-10-06 (BDC loan marks and Punctual Pros filings items 2026-09-24).
caveats: Almost no sponsor discloses entry or exit EV, EBITDA or MOIC. The only exit multiples in the multiple fields are press estimates: Champions ~18.5x (Bloomberg-cited) and Sila ~17x incl. pending acquisitions (HomePros). Apex ~20x and FGS ~19x are analyst arithmetic and stay out of the multiple fields.

revenue growth multiple uses only sourced before/after pairs or sponsor-stated multiples (TurnPoint ~10x, Smith + Howard ~4x, Sciens >35x, Shermco 2x, Teneo >2x); several are not like-for-like (perimeter changes, systemwide sales instead of revenue), as stated in each row note.

Timing statistics are small samples: first add-on n=11, cadence n=8, hold n=21. First-add-on months exclude cases whose earliest add-ons are missing from the sources (e.g. Apex, Sila under MSCP, Heartland).
Hold years measure the case's entry date to exit date, i.e. the first sponsor in the case fields (e.g. Odyssey for Champions, MSCP for Sila, GI Partners for Consilio).

VWR (cx-09) and Avantor (cx-10) share the 2017 transaction; both are kept and cross-linked. Wrench (case-wr) and Apex (case-ap) share Alpine's growth plan. Smith + Howard (cx-01) also appears as template items pn-tpl-* in pp_nationwide.json.
No case gives a sourced "share of customers on a membership" figure, so the membership pattern uses members per technician (Champions) and memberships per household served (Redwood/Sierra, derived).
Vendor case studies (ServiceTitan, Rilla) and benchmarks cross-referenced from ServiceOS evidence and Punctual Pros nationwide plan are selected customers or vendor data, not controlled studies.

Punctual Pros applicability, Punctual Pros next step and the Punctual Pros sequence are analyst recommendations, not company plans. Steps 0-2 are dated facts; steps 3-14 are proposed. Punctual Pros KPIs (members, booking rate, close rate) are not public and must come from its ServiceTitan.

dedup.note: No company appeared in both source files.

meta.narrative: Across 34 cases from 1996 to 2026, the companies that sold for the most did the same six things in roughly the same order, and Punctual Pros is now about 30 months into its own version of that sequence. First, the sponsor put an operator team in charge at entry: Alpine named Apex's CEO and CFO on launch day in July 2019 with $100M+ of committed equity, American Capital gave Service Experts' returning CEO about 10% ownership, and Huron recruited Sciens' CEO before it bought its first company. Second, the first add-on came early and close to home, a median of about 7 months after entry across 11 dated cases, as Smith + Howard did with Market Street Partners in month 9 and Punctual Pros did with Horvath in month 8. Third, the tuck-ins kept coming at roughly one every three to five months: Trivest did 16 at TurnPoint while revenue grew nearly 10x, Huron did 13 at Sciens while revenue and EBITDA rose more than 35x, and Broad Sky did nine at Smith + Howard while headcount went from about 100 to about 800. Fourth, every brand ran on one system: CenterOak ran a single IT system and consolidated purchasing at Service Champions, Wrench now books online at 99% of its locations on ServiceTitan, and Authority Brands moved Punctual Pros and every other One Hour, Benjamin Franklin and Mister Sparky location onto ServiceTitan in September 2024. Fifth, they built recurring revenue that buyers pay for: Champions grew from about 60,000 members in 2021 to about 150,000 in 2026 (about 71 to 83 per technician) and sold to Blackstone in February 2026 at a reported ~18.5x trailing EBITDA, while Frontdoor gets 76% of its revenue from renewals with 84% of customers on auto-pay. Sixth, they owned the technician pipeline: Champions more than doubled its field technicians from 850 to 1,800+, Shermco grew certified technicians from 400+ to 600+ as Gryphon doubled revenue and sold for about $1.6B, and Sila bought a trade school in January 2026. Margin beat volume in the best compounders, as VWR grew Adjusted EBITDA 8.6% a year against 3.7% sales growth from 2006 to 2013 and IES grew operating income 88% on 21% more revenue in FY2024. In the last 12-18 months before a sale the winners kept buying and published KPIs: Shermco closed five add-ons in the 17 months before Blackstone, Sila added four brands in the nine months before Goldman's ~$1.7B (~17x) purchase, and Smith + Howard disclosed more than 600 employees and ~$175M of expected revenue about five months before TPG signed. Most exits went to a larger sponsor, often with the seller or management rolling equity (Charlesbank into GI Partners at ARS, Odyssey alongside Blackstone at Champions, BV alongside Broad Sky at Frontline), and the median first-sponsor hold was about 4.4 years (4.0 in residential home services). The failures show what not to copy: Any Hour signed 16 partnerships in about 13 months and its loan now carries PIK at ~89% of par, TurnPoint grew from 17 to 65 brands and now pays PIK under a new CEO, Horizon is lender-supported, and Roto-Rooter's parent Chemed raised ad spend about $11M from 2023 to 2025 while segment revenue fell about $50M. For Punctual Pros the order is an integration leader and a ServiceTitan KPI pack now, members per technician as the north-star metric, one contiguous tuck-in per quarter in PA, NJ, MD and DE, a Lancaster academy with Thaddeus Stevens, leverage near the 2.9-3.3x lower-middle-market norm, and an exit-ready KPI pack by about 2028.

punctual_pros_sequence.anchor: Broad Sky entry 2024-04-03 = hold month 0; forward window 2026-10-01 to 2029-09-30 (36 months)

steps.action: Broad Sky acquires Punctual Pros (CEO Matt Buckwalter; the 2026 FDD lists 25 tri-brand territories, 19 PA and 6 NJ after Horvath).
ServiceTitan becomes the primary portfolio company across all One Hour, Benjamin Franklin and Mister Sparky locations, including PP.
Add-on #1: Horvath Home Services (Ocean and Monmouth Counties NJ), month 8 vs a case median of ~7 months.

Name an integration/operations leader and publish a weekly ServiceTitan KPI pack (booking rate, close rate, average ticket, members, members per technician, technicians, jobs) for PP and Horvath; write the 90-day tuck-in integration checklist from the Horvath experience.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: Inbound booking rate benchmark 38% (HVAC) -> 59% (25+ tech shops), serviceos kb-pp-1

steps.action: One Lancaster contact center for all brands: AI answering for overflow and after-hours calls, missed-call text-back, online booking on every brand site; measure cost per booked job by channel.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: Online booking share <5% industry baseline -> ~20% (Eco Plumbers), pn-lev-01

steps.action: Relaunch the membership program as the north-star metric: auto-pay by default, renewal agent on lapsing members, member offer on every repair ticket; report members per technician monthly.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: Members per technician toward Champions' ~83 (kb-pp-3); Frontdoor 84% auto-pay

steps.action: Price book and sales coaching: good/better/best flat-rate price book on every tablet, BuyMax purchasing, AI ride-along coaching for comfort advisors and technicians.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: Close rate +9% (Total Comfort/TurnPoint, kb-pp-4); average-ticket growth 8% vs 14% (kb-pp-2)

steps.action: Restart the tuck-in cadence: one contiguous deal per quarter inside the PA core and adjacent ring (Lancaster, York, Dauphin, Berks, Lebanon) and next to Horvath in NJ, each with 20-35% seller rollover and the 90-day checklist; include neighbouring tri-brand franchisees.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: ~4 add-ons in 2027 (case median ~4.6 months per deal; TurnPoint ~1 per quarter)

steps.action: Lancaster academy: Thaddeus Stevens partnership plus PA registered apprenticeships, paid earn-while-you-learn cohorts, published tech -> lead -> trainer -> manager ladder.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: HVAC technician turnover benchmark 16% a year (pn-pro-07); Champions doubled technicians in ~5 years

steps.action: Shared back office in Lancaster for every brand (AP/AR, permits, recruiting, marketing) and one parent identity for recruiting and seller outreach, keeping acquired local names co-branded during tri-brand conversion.
Attach adjacent lines to existing visits: generators via Mister Sparky, IAQ, water treatment; run the new-mover engine on deed data.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: Generac home-standby penetration ~6.5% of addressable homes (pn-lev-05)

steps.action: Fund the program: draw the delayed-draw term loan for tuck-ins, then size an incremental facility or refinancing to the larger company; keep leverage near the lower-middle-market norm and avoid PIK.

Exit preparation (12-18 months before a process): audited monthly KPI pack (members, members per technician, technicians, jobs a year, booking and close rates), quality of earnings, all brands on one system and one back office; keep buying.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: Exit multiples for scaled companies reported at ~17x (Sila, incl. pending deals) to ~18.5x (Champions) vs 6.3-6.9x for sub-$25M TEV deals

steps.action: Phase 3 metro anchor: buy one larger Mid-Atlantic company (Baltimore, Philadelphia suburbs or Pittsburgh, including franchise-to-franchise conversations such as Pittsburgh's 6-territory One Hour operator), funded with a Broad Sky co-invest SPV.
Exit window: sale to a larger sponsor with Broad Sky and management rolling equity, or a minority recap/continuation if the cadence is still compounding; launch with 1-2 tuck-ins signed or pending.
steps.kpi_or_benchmark: Case median hold ~4.4 years (n=21); residential/franchise median ~4.0 years (n=12)

items.sponsor: Chemed Corporation (public strategic owner; benchmark, not a PE case)

timeline.event: Chemed (already owner of ~58%) tenders for the ~42% of Roto-Rooter Inc. it did not own at $41.00 per share; the price was 17.8x Roto-Rooter's estimated 1996 earnings. Roto-Rooter was then the largest US sewer/drain cleaner, running company-owned and franchised operations (first franchise 1936).
timeline.metric: FY1995 revenue $179.8M; 17.8x est. 1996 earnings (P/E, not EBITDA)

timeline.event: Roto-Rooter buys back franchise territories; $59.2M of the 2019 purchase price was allocated to reacquired franchise rights.
Continues converting franchises to company-owned branches: South Carolina ($0.3M) and Georgia ($3.7M).
Buys franchises in New Jersey ($5.8M), Texas ($1.5M) and Kentucky ($5.1M).

FY2025 Roto-Rooter net revenue $899.9M (FY2024 $900.3M; FY2023 $949.4M). Chemed advertising expense (mostly pay-per-click and cost-per-call internet leads) rose to $83.1M from $72.2M in 2023. Implicit price concessions/credit memos rose 41.8% to $38.0M. 2025 plumbing growth came from a 3.6% higher job count offset by a 2.9% fall in price/mix.

Q4 2025: Roto-Rooter revenue $220.6M (-3.7%), Adjusted EBITDA $47.5M (-21.1%), margin 21.5%; residential revenue -3.1%, commercial +1.6%. 2026 guidance: revenue +3.0-3.5%, Adjusted EBITDA margin 22.5-23.0%.

kpi_before_after.period: FY1995 -> FY2025 (FY1995 total company; FY2025 segment net revenue)

items.what_broad_sky_can_copy: Roto-Rooter has spent 30 years buying back its own franchisees, so for Punctual Pros the parallel move is buying neighbouring One Hour, Ben Franklin and Mister Sparky territories inside the Authority system, as it did with Horvath. Roto-Rooter's 2023-2025 numbers are also a warning: Chemed's ad spend rose about $11M while segment revenue fell about $50M and price concessions jumped 42%, so PP should track cost per booked job and not just lead volume. That argues for owned demand (memberships, reviews, repeat customers) over rented demand (pay-per-click and cost-per-call leads).
items.data_notes: Public benchmark, not a sponsor case. FY2025 segment Adjusted EBITDA was not read directly from the 10-K, so exit EBITDA is null. FY1995 revenue is Roto-Rooter Inc. consolidated (it included equipment sales to franchisees).
items.confidence_basis: SEC 10-K and 1996 Schedule 14D-9 figures; public benchmark

items.sponsor: American Capital (2013-2016) -> Enercare (2016-2018) -> Brookfield Infrastructure (2018-)
items.exit_buyer: Enercare Inc. (later acquired by Brookfield Infrastructure, 2018)

timeline.event: Lennox divests Service Experts to American Capital. Scott Boxer returns as CEO with ~10% ownership. The plan: a 'leaner, flatter' organisation, a restored legacy local brand name on each branch instead of one uniform brand, and a target of 6-7% annual organic growth.
Moves from one uniform 'Service Experts' name back to co-branding branches with their 40-60-year-old legacy local names.
Enercare agrees to buy Service Experts (SEHAC Holdings) for US$340.75M. Service Experts then had 90 locations in 29 US states and 3 Canadian provinces.
Enercare completes the acquisition.

Under Brookfield, Service Experts (nearly US$1B revenue, 75+ corporate locations, 31 states) switches its main growth engine from M&A to franchising: 5 franchisees across 16 territories so far, ~15 expected by year-end across ~30 territories, then ~20 new franchisees a year. More than 50% of installs go through the 'Advantage' equipment-leasing subscription.

kpi_before_after.kpi: Share of installs on recurring leasing (Advantage)

items.what_broad_sky_can_copy: Service Experts doubled down on local brand equity (restoring legacy names) while centralising the back office, and that is the model for keeping Horvath's NJ name alive under Punctual Pros. Its leasing program, which carries over half of installs, shows that a financed or subscription offer can turn one-off replacement sales into recurring revenue that buyers value; PP should test an equipment-as-a-service offer on Lancaster replacements. Brookfield's shift from M&A to franchising also confirms that the franchise model PP already sits inside is scalable.
items.data_notes: American Capital's 2013 purchase price and Service Experts' revenue at either transaction were not disclosed in the sources read. The 2018 Brookfield-Enercare deal is a parent-level transaction; its date and terms were not re-verified in this pass. The 2026 revenue (~US$1B) and franchise figures come from a Mergermarket interview.
